title: Air & Rain Waterworks: A DIY Guide to Harvesting Rain, Dew, Fog, and Atmospheric Moisture
description: Your roof, your fog, and your meter are the data. This book shows you how to use them. Air & Rain Waterworks is a practical guide to catching water you can actually use. Rain off a roof. Runoff you keep on your own ground. Fog on a mesh. Dew on a cold sheet. Moisture a machine pulls from air. It is written for a careful beginner, and for a reader who already owns a tank, a pump, or a condenser and wants the method, not a slogan. You will learn how a design is determined. You will not be handed a universal gutter size, a wire size, a bleach recipe, a filter bed depth, or a guaranteed number of liters. The guide moves in that order: decide what the water is for, read the site, pick one method, then storage, treatment, pumps, and power. Troubleshooting sits with the job. Worked numbers are labeled Measured, Manufacturer-rated, Published, Assumed, or Estimated. A labeled example is not a recommendation for your house. What you can do with it Measure the water you use, and separate drinking from washing. Read a dry stretch as a stress test, not as the only way to size storage. Walk a roof path from the drip edge to the overflow, then commission it with a hose. Keep a site log for fog and dew, and refuse a yield copied from someone else's climate. Compare a machine's liters with the watt-hours your own meter shows. Size a tank with a worked month whose inputs are labeled. That month is an example, not your climate. Match treatment to the contaminant a test found. Know the stop lines: a borehole, a live circuit, a refrigerant line, a structural stand, and drainage that leaves your ground.
